extracted.intended_audience: students of natural history, naturalists, and educated general readers interested in evolution and species theory
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and explaining what constitutes a 'species' and what evidence or tests (e.g., hybridization, morphology, fossil record, distribution, development) should count for or against competing hypotheses about species origin (special creation vs transmutation/natural selection).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hybridization (physiological) test for species
rubrics_metrics.description: If a male and a female, selected from each group, produce offspring, and that offspring is fertile with others produced in the same way, the groups are races and not species. If, on the other hand, no result ensues, or if the offspring are infertile with others produced in the same way, they are true physiological species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage sets out the hybridization test in original wording but immediately cautions it is often impracticable and frequently yields ambiguous results. Practical obstacles: confinement can alter breeding behaviour, wild animals often refuse to mate in captivity, hermaphroditism and pollen-contamination complicate plant crosses, and long experiments are required to check fertility of hybrids. Even when applicable, reciprocal crosses may give different results; some 'varieties' are almost sterile when crossed and some presumed distinct species are perfectly fertile when crossed. Thus the test is useful in principle but limited and unreliable in many real cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Morphological species concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Living beings ... are divisible into multitudes of distinctly definable kinds, which are morphological species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion defines species by distinct and definable morphological (structural) characters. The text presents this as one of the principal ways naturalists classify organisms, distinct from physiological (breeding) groupings. No specific scoring rubric is given, but morphological distinctiveness is treated as an essential characteristic to recognize and delimit taxa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physiological (breeding) species concept
rubrics_metrics.description: They are also divisible into groups of individuals, which breed freely together, tending to reproduce their like, and are physiological species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion defines species by propensity to interbreed and reproduce like offspring. The author contrasts it with the morphological concept and notes that races (domesticated varieties) can mimic morphological species while still being physiologically inter-fertile; conversely, not all morphological differences imply reproductive isolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fertility/sterility as an unreliable and variable indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: The sterility is of all degrees, and is often so slight that the two most careful experimentalists ... have come to diametrically opposite conclusions in ranking forms by this test. The sterility is innately variable in individuals of the same species, and is eminently susceptible of favourable and unfavourable conditions. The degree of sterility does not strictly follow systematic affinity, but is governed by several curious and complex laws. It is generally different and sometimes widely different, in reciprocal crosses between the same two species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author (quoting Darwin) emphasizes many caveats: variability among individuals, environmental sensitivity, reciprocal-cross asymmetry, differences between first crosses and subsequent hybrid generations, parallels with grafting, and multiple causal factors (embryo death, disturbed reproductive systems). Examples include plants more fertile with other species' pollen than with their own and species with apparently contradictory cross-fertility patterns. The guidance is anti-pattern: do not over-rely on single crossing results; interpret hybridization outcomes cautiously and in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of groups absolutely incapable of fertile union (theoretical requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are such things in Nature as groups of animals and of plants, whose members are incapable of fertile union with those of other groups; and there are such things as hybrids, which are absolutely sterile when crossed with other hybrids. ... any theory of the origin of species ... would have to account for it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that any satisfactory theory of species origin must explain the empirical fact that some groups are reproductively isolated and that some hybrids are absolutely sterile. This is presented as a constraint on theoretical accounts (a desideratum): theories must account for the existence of reproductive isolation phenomena, not merely dismiss them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geological/fossil continuity as evidence against special creation
rubrics_metrics.description: The vast series of extinct animals and plants is not divisible ... into distinct groups, separated by sharply-marked boundaries. There are no great gulfs between epochs and formations--no successive periods marked by the appearance of plants, of water animals, and of land animals, 'en masse'. Every year adds to the list of links between what the older geologists supposed to be widely separated epochs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage uses fossil continuity, high percentages of shared genera between successive formations, and intermediate beds with mixed faunas (e.g., Maestricht, St. Cassian, lias beds) as empirical criteria that argue against episodic supernatural creation. Guidance: an acceptable origin theory should accommodate gradual change evidenced by the stratigraphic record and not require ad hoc miraculous interventions at many narrowly spaced intervals (anti-pattern: invoking special acts of creation to explain stratigraphic appearance of new species).

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical distribution patterns as evidentiary criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: The species of animals which inhabit the sea on opposite sides of the isthmus of Panama are wholly distinct; the animals and plants which inhabit islands are commonly distinct from those of the neighbouring mainlands, and yet have a similarity of aspect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patterns of distribution in space (e.g., island biogeography, disjunct faunas around geographic barriers like the isthmus of Panama) serve as criteria for evaluating hypotheses about species origin and dispersion. An adequate theory should explain why distinct but related forms cluster geographically and why islands often host distinct yet similar taxa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Developmental relations and homology (comparative embryology/anatomy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The singular phenomena brought to light by the study of development; the structural relations of species upon which our systems of classification are founded; the great doctrines of philosophical anatomy, such as that of homology, or of the community of structural plan exhibited by large groups of species differing very widely in their habits and functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similarity of developmental pathways and common structural plans (homologies) are treated as strong empirical criteria supporting common descent/transmutation and problematic for ad hoc special-creation accounts. Guidance: explanatory theories should account for conserved developmental patterns and homologous structures across diverse taxa; these facts count as positive evidence rather than incidental detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy with artificial selection/domestication as evidential support
rubrics_metrics.description: All species have been produced by the development of varieties from common stocks; by the conversion of these, first into permanent races and then into new species, by the process of 'natural selection', which process is essentially identical with that artificial selection by which man has originated the races of domestic animals--the 'struggle for existence' taking the place of man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of domestication/artificial selection as a model: if artificial selection can produce distinct races by selective pressure, a natural analogous selective process (natural selection) operating in the struggle for existence is offered as a criterion/mechanism that a theory must plausibly deploy. Guidance: analogical reasoning from human-bred varieties is legitimate evidence for mechanisms of change, but the text implies this must be supplemented by additional lines of evidence (fossils, distribution, homology).

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Vera causa' (true cause) requirement for hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Lamarck ... felt that mere speculation was not the way to arrive at the origin of species, but that it was necessary ... to discover by observation or otherwise, some 'vera causa', competent to give rise to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This methodological criterion demands that any scientific hypothesis about species origin identify actual, demonstrable causal agents capable of producing the observed changes (not mere assertion). Anti-pattern: accepting speculative causes without observational/experimental justification. The text praises Lamarck's insistence on vera causa even while criticizing his particular proposed cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance of sufficient time as a methodological requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: He insisted on the necessity of allowing sufficient time, very strongly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A viable theory of species origin must plausibly allow adequate temporal scales for gradual modifications and the accumulation of changes. This is presented as a necessary auxiliary assumption: without sufficient time, naturalistic mechanisms cannot plausibly account for observed diversity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformitarian principle (explain past by existing causes)
rubrics_metrics.description: We must look to existing causes for the explanation of past geological events. ... when the mind has once admitted the conception of the gradual production of the present physical state of our globe, by natural causes operating through long ages of time, it will be little disposed to allow that living beings have made their appearance in another way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion favors explanations that employ processes observable today (uniformitarianism) over extraordinary or supernatural interventions. Guidance: hypotheses should appeal to known natural laws and processes extended through time rather than invoking unique supernatural acts; the text frames this as a historical-geological methodological standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of argument from ignorance / supernatural explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: This sort of reasoning is an 'argumentum ad ignorantiam'--take this explanation or be ignorant. ... The supernatural interposition of the Creator can, by the nature of the case, exemplify no law, and if species have really arisen in this way, it is absurd to attempt to discuss their origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a normative criterion for explanatory acceptability: do not accept supernatural explanations that do not exemplify general laws and provide no causal account. Instead prefer explanations that render phenomena instances of known natural laws. Anti-pattern: substituting 'it pleases God' or similar deus ex machina reasoning for empirical explanation.
